Project Overview¶

Motivation¶

A nutritious and balanced diet is one of the most important things for a healthy lifestyle. However, this can be a tedious task; one must count all the nutrient values of the ingredients used in their meal, and also estimate how certain preparation processes (such as stir-frying, deep-frying, boiling, etc.) can affect it. It is also not an exact science, as exact quantities of foods usually aren't measured. A convenient workaround would be to take images of a meal and process them through a learned model that can make rough predictions on certain amounts of nutrients in the meal, such as calories, carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.

Our Solution¶

We propose to use the power of transfer learning to build a lightweight convolutional neural network that can predict amounts of calories (kcal), carbohydrates (g), proteins (g), and fat (g).

Our project can be broken down in the following steps:

  1. We use a ResNet152 model pre-trained on the Food-2K dataset (provided here) with the last layer removed, and then we pass images from the Food-100K dataset to this model to extract 2048-dimensional features. All the steps here can be found in the file feature_extraction.ipynb in the provided github link.

  2. Train a regression model with 4 output neurons, using the extracted features from step 1). This model makes predictions on: 1) calories (kcal), 2) protein (g), 3) carbohydrates (g), 4) fat (g)

  3. Test on unseen images from the dataset, as well as new images with human annotated nutritional information, as well as comparing against a baseline method.

Our pipeline can be summarized in the image below:

Step 1c. Cast nutrition data to float and add to the dataset¶

As the dataset exists, it has one column for "nutritional_profile" which has all the names and values as a string. Extract calories, carbohydrates, proteins, and fats separately into their own feature column.

In [ ]:
def get_nutrition(example, string):
    """
    Extracts calories, carbohydates, proteins, and fats from the nutritional_profile feature as numeric values
    """
    profile = example['nutritional_profile']
    # Split the string to get the nutrient name (e.g., 'carbohydrate')
    nutrition_name = string.split('_')[0]

    # if it's a string, parse it to a dict
    if isinstance(profile, str):
        try:
            profile = json.loads(profile.replace("'", '"'))
        except:
            return {nutrition_name: None}

    # extract the specific nutritional value using the full string (e.g., 'calories_kcal')
    nutrition_amt = profile.get(string)
    return {nutrition_name: float(nutrition_amt) if nutrition_amt is not None else None}

Now plot histograms and box-and-whisker plots for the values. It is important to identify if the distributions are skewed and if outliers may affect the data

In [ ]:
def plot_statistics(stat, unit):
  nutrients = dataset['train'][stat]
  stat = stat.capitalize()

  fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 6))

  # Histogram
  ax1.hist(nutrients, bins=40, color='skyblue', edgecolor='black', alpha=0.7)
  ax1.set_title(f'Histogram of {stat}', fontsize=14)
  ax1.set_xlabel(f'{stat} ({unit})', fontsize=12)
  ax1.set_ylabel('Frequency', fontsize=12)
  ax1.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)

  # Box Plot
  ax2.boxplot(nutrients, vert=False, patch_artist=True,
              boxprops=dict(facecolor='lightgreen', color='black'),
              medianprops=dict(color='red', linewidth=2))
  ax2.set_title(f'Box Plot of {stat}', fontsize=14)
  ax2.set_xlabel(f'{stat} ({unit})', fontsize=12)
  # ax2.set_yticklabels(['Training Set'])
  ax2.grid(axis='x', linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)

  plt.suptitle(f'{stat} Distribution Analysis (MM-Food-100K)', fontsize=16, fontweight='bold')
  plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.03, 1, 0.95])
  plt.show()

def plot_histogram(stat):
  nutrients = dataset['train'][stat]
  log_nutrients = np.log1p(np.array(nutrients))

  plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
  plt.hist(log_nutrients, bins=40, color='salmon', edgecolor='black', alpha=0.7)

  plt.title('Histogram of Log-Transformed Calories', fontsize=14)
  plt.xlabel('Log(1 + Calories)', fontsize=12)
  plt.ylabel('Frequency', fontsize=12)
  plt.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)

  plt.show()

Step 2. Build neural network model¶

In [ ]:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision import models
import torch.optim as optim

Our model is a simple dense linear model. it takes in as input the 2048-dimensional features pre-computed by the ResNet152 pre-trained on Food2K. The neurons in the layers are 2048 $\rightarrow$ 512 $\rightarrow$ 256 $\rightarrow$ 4. ReLu is used as the nonlinear activation function, batch normalization is used in the 512 layers, and dropout of 30% is performed afterwards.

In [ ]:
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
print("Using device:", device)

class NutritionPredictor(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim=2048, output_dim=4):
        super(NutritionPredictor, self).__init__()
        self.name = 'nutrition_predictor_dropout_256'
        self.regressor = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, 512),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(512),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Dropout(0.3),

            nn.Linear(512, 256),
            nn.ReLU(),

            nn.Linear(256, output_dim)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.regressor(x)

model = NutritionPredictor().to(device)

Step 3. Create Helper Functions.¶

These include the training/evaluating functions as well as plotters for the training curves, and getting model names based on hyperparameter combinations

In [ ]:
def get_model_name(name, batch_size, learning_rate, epoch):
    """
    Generate a name for the model consisting of all the hyperparameter values

    Params
    ----------
    name: model name

    """
    path = "model_{0}_bs{1}_lr{2}_epoch{3}".format(name, batch_size, learning_rate, epoch)
    return path

def plot_training_curve(path, return_val_error=False, model_name=''):

    NUTRIENT_KEYS = ['calories_kcal', 'carbohydrate_g', 'fat_g', 'protein_g']

    train_err = np.loadtxt(f"{path}_train_err.csv")
    val_err   = np.loadtxt(f"{path}_val_err.csv")

    if return_val_error:
        return val_err[-1]

    epochs = range(1, len(train_err) + 1)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
    fig.suptitle(f'Train vs Validation Error ({model_name})')
    axes = axes.flatten()

    for i, (ax, key) in enumerate(zip(axes, NUTRIENT_KEYS)):
        ax.plot(epochs, train_err[:, i], label='Train')
        ax.plot(epochs, val_err[:, i],   label='Validation')
        ax.set_title(key)
        ax.set_xlabel('Epoch')
        ax.set_ylabel('Error')
        ax.legend()

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Helpers for evaluating and training (Label is log transformed)¶

In [ ]:
def evaluate_transfer_net_with_log(net, loadername, feature_dir, criterion):
    device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
    total_mae = torch.zeros(4).to(device)
    total_samples = 0
    net = net.to(device)
    net.eval()
    norms = NORMS.to(device)

    all_preds = []
    all_labels = []

    feature_files = [f for f in os.listdir(feature_dir) if f.startswith(loadername) and f.endswith('.pt')]

    with torch.no_grad():
        for i in range(len(feature_files)):
            file_path = os.path.join(feature_dir, f'{loadername}_{i}.pt')
            if not os.path.exists(file_path): continue

            features, labels = torch.load(file_path)
            features = features.to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device).float()

            outputs = net(features) # model output is in Log space

            # Convert both to calorie
            # predictions = torch.expm1(outputs)
            preds_raw  = outputs * norms
            labels_raw = labels  * norms

            # abs_error = torch.abs(predictions - raw_calories)

            # all_preds.extend(predictions.cpu().numpy())
            # all_labels.extend(raw_calories.cpu().numpy())
            total_mae     += torch.abs(preds_raw - labels_raw).sum(dim=0)
            total_samples += labels.shape[0]

            all_preds.extend(preds_raw.cpu().numpy())
            all_labels.extend(labels_raw.cpu().numpy())

            # total_mae += abs_error.sum().item()
            # total_samples += len(labels)

    avg_mae = (total_mae / total_samples).cpu().numpy() if total_samples > 0 else 0
    return avg_mae, all_labels, all_preds
In [ ]:
NORMS = torch.tensor([3500, 250, 250, 650])  # calories, protein, fat, carbs
NUTRIENT_KEYS = ['calories_kcal', 'protein_g','fat_g','carbohydrate_g']

def train_transfer_net_with_log(net, feature_dir, checkpoint_dir, batch_size=32, learning_rate=0.001, num_epochs=5):
    device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
    net = net.to(device)
    norms = NORMS.to(device)

    # --- Resuming training logic ---
    start_epoch = 0
    existing_files = [f for f in os.listdir(checkpoint_dir)
                      if f.startswith(f'model_{net.name}_bs{batch_size}_lr{learning_rate}')
                      and not f.endswith('.csv')]

    if existing_files:
        try:
            epochs_found = []
            for f in existing_files:
                parts = f.split('epoch')[-1]
                num = ''.join(filter(str.isdigit, parts))
                if num:
                    epochs_found.append(int(num))

            if epochs_found:
                last_epoch = max(epochs_found)
                load_path = os.path.join(checkpoint_dir, get_model_name(net.name, batch_size, learning_rate, last_epoch))
                print(f'Found data! Loading Epoch {last_epoch}. Resuming from {last_epoch + 1}...')
                net.load_state_dict(torch.load(load_path))
                start_epoch = last_epoch + 1
        except Exception as e:
            print(f'Error parsing files: {e}. Starting from 0.')
    else:
        print(f'No matching files found. Starting from 0.')

    # --- Training logic ---
    criterion = nn.MSELoss()
    optimizer = optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)

    end_epoch = start_epoch + num_epochs
    train_mae = np.zeros((end_epoch, 4))
    val_mae   = np.zeros((end_epoch, 4))

    if start_epoch > 0:
        old_model_path = os.path.join(checkpoint_dir, get_model_name(net.name, batch_size, learning_rate, last_epoch))
        try:
            train_mae[:start_epoch] = np.atleast_1d(np.loadtxt(f'{old_model_path}_train_err.csv'))
            val_mae[:start_epoch] = np.atleast_1d(np.loadtxt(f'{old_model_path}_val_err.csv'))
            print(f'Successfully loaded history for {start_epoch} epochs.')
        except Exception as e:
            print(f'Could not load CSV history: {e}')

    train_files = [f for f in os.listdir(feature_dir) if f.startswith('train_') and f.endswith('.pt')]

    for epoch in range(start_epoch, end_epoch):
        net.train()
        total_mae = torch.zeros(4).to(device)
        total_samples = 0

        for i in range(len(train_files)):
            file_path = os.path.join(feature_dir, f'train_{i}.pt')
            if not os.path.exists(file_path): continue

            features, labels = torch.load(file_path)
            features = features.to(device)
            # labels = labels.to(device).view(-1, 1).float() # labels are 0-1 from feature extraction
            labels = labels.to(device).float()


            # --- Log transformation ---
            # raw_calories = labels * 3500.0
            # log_labels = torch.log1p(raw_calories)
            # loss = criterion(outputs, log_labels)

            # loss = criterion(outputs, log_labels) # output is in Log space
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            outputs = net(features)
            loss = criterion(outputs, labels)  # train directly on normalized labels
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()


            # --- Convert back to calories ---
            # predictions = torch.expm1(outputs)
            # total_mae += torch.abs(predictions - raw_calories).sum().item()
            # total_samples += len(labels)

            preds_raw  = outputs.detach() * norms
            labels_raw = labels * norms
            total_mae     += torch.abs(preds_raw - labels_raw).sum(dim=0)
            total_samples += labels.shape[0]

        # --- Save results ---
        train_mae[epoch] = (total_mae / total_samples).cpu().numpy()
        # val_mae[epoch], _, _ = evaluate_transfer_net_with_log(net, 'val', feature_dir, criterion)
        val_mae[epoch], _, _ = evaluate_transfer_net_with_log(net, 'val', feature_dir, criterion)

        # print(f'Epoch {epoch}: Train MAE {train_mae[epoch]:.1f} | Val MAE {val_mae[epoch]:.1f} (Cals)')
        print(f'Epoch {epoch}:')
        for key, tr, va in zip(NUTRIENT_KEYS, train_mae[epoch], val_mae[epoch]):
            unit = 'kcal' if 'kcal' in key else 'g'
            print(f'  {key:<22} Train MAE: {tr:.2f} {unit}  |  Val MAE: {va:.2f} {unit}')

        model_path = os.path.join(checkpoint_dir, get_model_name(net.name, batch_size, learning_rate, epoch))
        torch.save(net.state_dict(), model_path)
        np.savetxt(f'{model_path}_train_err.csv', train_mae[:epoch+1])
        np.savetxt(f'{model_path}_val_err.csv', val_mae[:epoch+1])

Step 4. Training¶

Many iterations of hyperparameters were tested. The best results were achieved with:

  • batch_size: 128
  • learning_rate: 0.001
  • epochs: 63

Step 5. Make predictions.¶

With the trained model, make predictions on the test dataset, as well as new curated images.

Step 5a. Load the model¶

In [ ]:
transfer_model_path = os.path.join(checkpoint_dir,
                                   get_model_name('nutrition_predictor_dropout_256', batch_size=bs, learning_rate=lr, epoch=num_epoch))

model = NutritionPredictor()
model.load_state_dict(torch.load(transfer_model_path))
model.eval()
Out[ ]:
NutritionPredictor(
  (regressor): Sequential(
    (0): Linear(in_features=2048, out_features=512, bias=True)
    (1): BatchNorm1d(512, eps=1e-05, momentum=0.1, affine=True, track_running_stats=True)
    (2): ReLU()
    (3): Dropout(p=0.3, inplace=False)
    (4): Linear(in_features=512, out_features=256, bias=True)
    (5): ReLU()
    (6): Linear(in_features=256, out_features=4, bias=True)
  )
)

Step 5b. Evaluate on test data¶

First, get raw MAE outputs for each of calories, carbohydrates, fat, and protein

In [ ]:
criterion = nn.MSELoss()
test_mae, y_true, y_pred = evaluate_transfer_net_with_log(model, 'test', feature_dir, criterion)

NUTRIENT_KEYS = ['calories_kcal','protein_g','fat_g','carbohydrate_g'] # Redefine here for clarity, assuming it's available in global scope if not. Otherwise, ensure it is available.

print('--- Test MAE ---')
for i, key in enumerate(NUTRIENT_KEYS):
    unit = 'kcal' if 'kcal' in key else 'g'
    print(f'  {key:<22} MAE: {test_mae[i]:.2f} {unit}')

--- Test MAE ---
  calories_kcal          MAE: 141.74 kcal
  protein_g              MAE: 9.84 g
  fat_g                  MAE: 7.95 g
  carbohydrate_g         MAE: 17.23 g

Calculate median and mean nutrient statistics to contextualize the error as a percentage of these statistics

In [ ]:
median_nutrients = [cal_stats['50%'], carb_stats['50%'], fat_stats['50%'], protein_stats['50%']]
median_nutrients = [float(nut) for nut in median_nutrients]
mean_nutrients = [cal_stats['mean'], carb_stats['mean'], fat_stats['mean'], protein_stats['mean']]
mean_nutrients = [float(nut) for nut in mean_nutrients]

err_percent = (test_mae / mean_nutrients) * 100
err_percent
test_data = np.array([test_mae, mean_nutrients, err_percent]).T
In [ ]:
test_df = pd.DataFrame(data=test_data, index=NUTRIENT_KEYS, columns=['Test MAE', 'Mean', 'Test MAE (% of mean)'])
test_df

Visualize some results: input images along with predicted and actual nutrient values

In [ ]:
import random

random.seed(42)
num_images = 5

NUTRIENT_LABELS = ['Calories (kcal)', 'Protein (g)', 'Fat (g)', 'Carbs (g)']
norms = NORMS.cpu().numpy()

# Load all test features
all_features, all_labels = [], []
for f in sorted(os.listdir(feature_dir)):
    if f.startswith('test_') and f.endswith('.pt'):
        feats, labs = torch.load(os.path.join(feature_dir, f))
        all_features.append(feats)
        all_labels.append(labs)

all_features = torch.cat(all_features, dim=0)
all_labels = torch.cat(all_labels, dim=0)

# Pick random samples and run model
indices = random.sample(range(len(all_features)), num_images)

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    preds  = (model(all_features[indices].to(device)) * NORMS.to(device)).cpu().numpy()
    labels = (all_labels[indices] * NORMS).numpy()

# Plot
test_images = dataset['test'].cast_column('image_url', HFImage())
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, num_images, figsize=(5 * num_images, 6))

for ax, idx, pred, true in zip(axes, indices, preds, labels):
    ax.imshow(test_images[idx]['image_url'])
    ax.axis('off')
    title = f"           Actual   Pred\nCalories:  {true[0]:.0f}   {pred[0]:.0f} kcal\nProtein:   {true[1]:.1f}   {pred[1]:.1f}g\nFat:       {true[2]:.1f}   {pred[2]:.1f}g\nCarbs:     {true[3]:.1f}   {pred[3]:.1f}g"
    ax.set_title(title)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Step 5c. Augmented Data¶

We also performed testing on augmented data with the following augmentations:

  • SmallestMaxSize: Standardizes every image by resizing the smallest side to 512 pixels, preserving the original aspect ratio to prevent distortion.
  • Affine Transform: A comprehensive geometric operation that performs simultaneous translation (shifting the food left/right/up/down), rotation (tilting between -45° and 45°), and scaling (zoom in/out by 0.8x to 1.2x).
  • Random Resized Crop: Selects a random crop (40% to 100% of the original area) and scales it back to 512x512. This simulates zooming in on specific ingredients or plates.
  • Horizontal & Vertical Flips: Mirrored reflections of the images. Since food does not have a "correct" left-to-right orientation, this effectively doubles your effective data diversity.

Step 6. Discussion and Results¶

As can be seen by the results above, the model performs reasonably well in predicting calories and protein counts as a relative percentage of the mean. However, the model performs worse on fat, and very poor on carbohydrate estimation, with an MAE of over 80% of the mean.

However, given the context of nutrition estimation and our method, we believe these to be reasonable estimations

  • Nutrition Counting - getting precise nutritional amounts in a meal is not an exact science. For example, measurements of ingredients is not precise. One can cut a reasonable amount of bell pepper or chicken into their meal with a rough estimate of the amount of grams without weighing them. On top of that, certain methods alter the nutritional values (e.g. boiling dissolves water-soluble vitamins), and the exact amount and temperature of these processes also aren't precise when cooking. Even identical foods can have varying nutrition due to soil conditions, ripeness, storage, and more. People also may store food differently and for different amounts of time which also affect the nutritional composition.
  • Using single images - our project aims for convenience while performing reasonably accurate. Its main purpose is to get a reasonable amount of key nutritional values that anyone can reasonably use just by taking one image of a meal. It's also important to note that in computer, a single monocular image itself is not sufficient for deeper tasks, such as depth estimation and 3D reconstruction (e.g. SFM, NERF, Gaussian Splatting) which require multiple images. 3D volumetric data would provide far richer data for estimating amounts of food, which can guide more accurate estimation of nutritional amounts. Going directly from one image to regressed values is not the most expressive pipeline for estimation.

Given the reasons above, we believe the model performs reasonably as expected. Furthermore, carybohydrates (the worst performing value) is a complex macronutrient, which can be broken down into fibers and sugars, which are all affected by different cooking methods. Carbohydrates are also difficult to "measure" as they are done by calculating the difference between 100g of food and the amounts of water, protein, fat, ash, and alcohol per the USDA, where measurement errors can accumulate from the latter quantities. Per the Canadian Food Inspection Agency CFIA), there is a 20% error tolerance on nutritional amounts for packaged foods, showing that even with all the necessary regulations, laboratory preparation and measurement tools, there is an amount of uncertainty in nutritional contents.

It is also important to note that the nutritional amounts don't seem to represent continuous values, but rather "bins" that are half of the second least significant digit. For example, for values in the magnitude of hundreds, they will be 100, 150, 200, 250, etc. which is fairly coarse and subject to errors.

Appendix: Related Works and Citations.¶

Our primary work focused on training on features derived from the Food-100K dataset [1] with pre-training on the Food2K dataset [2]. There are also other widely-used food datasets, such as Food-101 [3], which is used for discriminative task (classification of 101 food categories given images).

There are also easy to use online tools, such as here, where you can input the recipe to get estimated amounts of nutritional profile. However, the purpose of our project is to have an easy solution to estimate these amounts simply by taking a photo of a meal, instead of tediously calculating all the amounts, which is time-consuming.

Future Work¶

We believe our project is a simple method that can produce reasonable estimates of nutritional information given an image of a meal, which is simple to gather and requires little pre-processing. For future works, there are multiple avenues to explore:

  • Use language embedding to guide prediction. The Food100K dataset provides other features, such as dish name and cooking methods (e.g. pan-frying, deep-frying) which can guide the nutrition estimation. For example, one can reasonably associate deep-frying with higher calories and fats compared to boiling.
  • Estimate amount of food. Instead of directly regressing to nutritional information, we can also try to estimate amounts of food to guide the estimation. This can be done with some heuristics, or aided with methods such as instance segmentation to get finer details about elements in the image.
  • Estimate more specific nutritional amounts. If portions of the ingredients can be estimated reasonably, these can be used in tabulated datasets of food (example) for a fine-grained breakdown of the nutritional values. For example, instead of just fat, it will estimate saturated, monosaturated, and polysatured fats, and carbohydrates can be broken down into fiber and sugar.
  • We can also perform image segmentation on the individual ingredients of the meal, such as in [4] (example outputs shown in the image below) and use these segmented instances to estimate the portion amount which can be used to estimate calorie amount.
